claim: Lis1-MUT mice display heterotopic banding of the principal cell layer in hippocampal area CA1
source: In coronal sections from dorsal hippocampus Lis1-MUT animals displayed heterotopic banding of the principal cell layer (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A showing the banding pattern

claim: Most Lis1-MUT animals display the strongest banding in area CA1, with fewer mice showing multiple PCLs past region CA2
source: Most animals displayed the strongest banding in area CA1, with fewer mice showing multiple PCLs past region CA2.
evidence: This is a direct observational statement from the manuscript describing the spatial distribution of banding

claim: Region CA3 rarely appeared banded in Lis1-MUT mice, but instead scattered and uncompacted
source: Region CA3 rarely appeared banded, but instead scattered and uncompacted.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript

claim: In Lis1-MUT mice, superficial bands were positioned between ~250–320 μm and deeper heterotopic bands were between ~100 and 190 μm
source: In Lis1-MUT mice, superficial bands were positioned between ~250–320 μm and deeper heterotopic bands (positioned closer to the alveus) were between ~100 and 190 μm.
evidence: Quantitative measurements of band positions are provided

claim: The entirety of normal wild type PCLs were located between ~175–300 μm from the border of the alveus and the cortex radially
source: In measuring from the border of the alveus and the cortex radially (toward radiatum, known as the radial axis of CA1), the entirety of normal wild type (Wt) PCLs were located between ~175–300 μm.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of wild-type PCL position

claim: Calbindin is expressed in superficial principal cells in several species
source: In addition to marking a subpopulation of GABAergic cells, calbindin is expressed in superficial principal cells in several species (Slomianka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: Lis1 wild-type litter mates show calbindin-expression among superficial principal cells of CA1
source: Consistent with these reports, our Lis1 wild-type litter mates show calbindin-expression among superficial principal cells of CA1 (Figure 1B, left).
evidence: Direct observation supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Calbindin staining in Lis1-MUT mice showed a strong bias for calbindin-expressing principal cells to occupy the deeper heterotopic principal cell layer
source: Conversely, calbindin staining in Lis1-MUT mice showed a strong bias for calbindin-expressing principal cells to occupy the deeper heterotopic principal cell layer (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Direct observation from immunohistochemistry experiments shown in Figure 1B

claim: In distal CA1 of Lis1-MUT mice, 18.0 ± 2.8% of cells in the deep layer express calbindin compared to 4.4 ± 1.0% in the superficial layer
source: Counts represent number of identified calbindin soma divided by number of DAPI identified cells, Wt: deep 8.9 ± 2.8%, superficial 25.1 ± 1.3%; Lis1-MUT: deep 18.0 ± 2.8%, superficial 4.4 ± 1.0%.
evidence: Quantitative data from cell counting experiments

claim: In distal CA1 of wild-type mice, 8.9 ± 2.8% of cells in the deep layer express calbindin compared to 25.1 ± 1.3% in the superficial layer
source: Counts represent number of identified calbindin soma divided by number of DAPI identified cells, Wt: deep 8.9 ± 2.8%, superficial 25.1 ± 1.3%; Lis1-MUT: deep 18.0 ± 2.8%, superficial 4.4 ± 1.0%.
evidence: Quantitative data from cell counting experiments

claim: The calbindin staining pattern in Lis1-MUT mice is not a general feature of having the Lis1 mutant allele, as animals with less severe banding display relatively normal, superficial calbindin soma positioning
source: This finding was not a general feature of having the Lis1 mutant allele, as in animals with less severe banding (or in the same slices nearer CA2) but still carrying the mutant Pafah1b1 allele, the PCL displayed relatively normal, superficial calbindin soma positioning (Figure 1F; Proximal CA1 Wt: deep 16.3 ± 2.3%; superficial 30.0 ± 2.0%; Lis1-MUT: deep 12.1 ± 2.3%; superficial 19.0 ± 2.4%, n = 12 and 11, respectively).
evidence: Comparison of calbindin positioning in regions with different degrees of banding severity

claim: A large proportion of the principal cells expressing calbindin are being preferentially shifted into the deeper heterotopic band in Lis1-MUT mice
source: A large proportion of the principal cells expressing calbindin are being preferentially shifted into the deeper heterotopic band, but it should be noted that calbindin cells overall still represent a minority of the population in either location.
evidence: Summary statement based on the quantitative data presented

claim: Principal cells are generated near what becomes the alveus and migrate radially during embryonic development in a deep to superficial manner
source: Given that principal cells are generated near what becomes the alveus and migrate radially during embryonic development in a deep to superficial manner (Caviness and Sidman, 1973; Angeivine, 1965; Stanfield and Cowan, 1979), the calbindin staining pattern suggested a late born population undergoing migratory failure in the Lis1-MUT mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The calbindin staining pattern suggests a late born population undergoing migratory failure in the Lis1-MUT mouse
source: Given that principal cells are generated near what becomes the alveus and migrate radially during embryonic development in a deep to superficial manner (Caviness and Sidman, 1973; Angeivine, 1965; Stanfield and Cowan, 1979), the calbindin staining pattern suggested a late born population undergoing migratory failure in the Lis1-MUT mouse.
evidence: Inference based on known developmental patterns and observed calbindin positioning

claim: Superficial principal cells in normal mice arise near the end of gestation (Embryonic days 16–17)
source: Superficial principal cells in normal mice arise near the end of gestation (Emb days 16–17) (Slomianka et al., 2011; Caviness and Sidman, 1973; Angeivine, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Approximately 10% of cells born on E12-E13 expressed calbindin at P30 in both wild-type and Lis1-MUT mice
source: Approximately 10% of cells born on E12-E13 expressed calbindin at P30 (Figure 2D; Wt: 9 ± 3%; Lis1-MUT: 12 ± 3%, n = 95 cells and 168 labeled cells analyzed from five animals, respectively) in both Lis1 wild-type littermates and mutants.
evidence: Quantitative data from birth-dating experiments

claim: Cells born E14-E15 co-stained for calbindin 42 ± 9% of the time for wild type and 52 ± 8% for Lis1 mutants
source: Cells born E14-E15 co-stained for calbindin 42 ± 9% of the time for wild type and 52 ± 8% (n = 221 and n = 128, from 10 animals) for Lis1 mutants
evidence: Quantitative data from birth-dating experiments

claim: Cells born E16-E17 co-stained for calbindin 54 ± 7% of the time for wild type and 71 ± 9% for Lis1 mutants
source: cells born E16-E17 co-stained for calbindin 54 ± 7% of the time for wild type and 71 ± 9% for Lis1 mutants (n = 48 and 20 labelled cells from 11 animals).
evidence: Quantitative data from birth-dating experiments

claim: The timing of calbindin cell birthdates remained similar to littermate controls in Lis1-MUT animals in that calbindin cells arise late in embryonic development
source: While the timing of calbindin cell birthdates remained similar to littermate controls in Lis1-MUT animals in that calbindin cells arise late in embryonic development (Figure 2D), positioning of these cells differed substantially.
evidence: Summary of birth-dating data comparing wild-type and mutant mice

claim: Later born cells positioned more superficially in wild-type littermates while they positioned more deeply in Lis1-MUT mice
source: Later born cells positioned more superficially in wild-type littermates (smaller PCL depth measurements), while they positioned more deeply in mutant mice (Figure 2E and F,E represents counts from single experiments data are averages and summarized in F).
evidence: Quantitative positional data from birth-dating experiments

claim: Deeply positioned calbindin-expressing cells in the Lis1-MUT mice are the same late-born cell population that are now ectopically positioned in the deeper heterotopic band
source: These results suggest that deeply positioned calbindin-expressing cells in the Lis1-MUT mice are the same late-born cell population that are now ectopically positioned in the deeper heterotopic band.
evidence: Inference based on birth-dating and positioning data

claim: Calbindin-expressing principal cells have more complex apical dendritic trees (more branching) than calbindin-negative counterparts
source: In particular, calbindin-expressing principal cells have more complex apical dendritic trees (more branching), than calbindin-negative counterparts (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: K-means clustering of morphological features is greater than 90% accurate as verified by mRNA and in situ hybridization approaches
source: A prior study using this approach suggested that clustering was greater than 90% accurate as verified by mRNA and in situ hybridization approaches but comes with the drawback that every recording must be histologically processed, virtually reconstructed, and analyzed (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: Relatively simple and complex cell morphologies persist in the Lis1 mutant, in approximately the same proportions to wild type mice
source: The data show that relatively simple and complex cell morphologies persist in the Lis1 mutant, in approximately the same proportions to wild type mice, with nearly overlapping cluster centers (complex cells, Wt: [−0.1, 0.8], Lis1-MUT: [−0.4, 0.9]; simple cells, Wt: [−1.8,–1.3], Lis1-MUT: [−1.7,–1.2]).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of morphological clustering data

claim: Complex cells were located superficial to simple cells in normal type controls and scattered but generally deeper than simple cells in Lis1-MUT mice
source: Grouping cells by the assigned shape cluster and plotting the associated PCL depth measurements (from the border between the first PCL and the radiatum) gives further support to the sorting results, as complex cells were located superficial to simple cells in normal type controls and scattered but generally deeper than simple cells in Lis1-MUT mice, in agreement with our calbindin staining experiment (Figure 3D PCL depth, Wt complex: 35 ± 8.0 μm, simple: 50.2 ± 6.3 μm, n = 13 and 11; Lis1-MUT, complex: 127 ± 23.4 μm, simple: 94.6 ± 12.3 μm, n = 8 and 13).
evidence: Quantitative positional data from morphologically classified cells

claim: Complex cells in both mutant and non-mutant animals tended to have their first prominent apical branch bifurcation points sooner than simple cells
source: Additionally, we observed that complex cells in both mutant and non-mutant animals tended to have their first prominent apical branch bifurcation points sooner than simple cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis

claim: The complex apical branch morphology can still be used to identify putative calbindin-expressing principal cells in Lis1-MUT mice
source: This suggests that the complex apical branch morphology can still be used to identify putative calbindin-expressing principal cells in Lis1-MUT mice.
evidence: Inference based on morphological analysis and calbindin expression patterns

claim: Out of eight successful recoveries from Calb1-cre:Ai14 mice, four principal cells with confirmed calbindin expression had LRI and ORI values in the upper right (complex) quadrant
source: Out of eight successful recoveries, four principal cells with confirmed calbindin expression had LRI and ORI values in the upper right (complex) quadrant (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: Direct experimental validation using genetically labeled calbindin cells

claim: Calbindin-expression remains predictive of the complex morphological group in Lis1-MUT mice
source: These data support the notion that relatively complex and simple morphologies persist in the Lis1 mutant, and calbindin-expression remains predictive of the complex morphological group.
evidence: Summary of morphological and genetic labeling data

claim: Wild-type complex cells typically have peak sholl intersections of 8–11 around 200 μm from the soma
source: While wild-type complex cells typically have peak sholl intersections of 8–11 around 200 μm from the soma, Lis1-MUT complex cells have fewer peak intersections (~7), closer to the soma (~125 μm) (Wt n = 10 complex and 14 simple; Lis1-MUT n = 10 complex and 12 simple).
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis using Sholl analysis

claim: Lis1-MUT complex cells have fewer peak sholl intersections (~7), closer to the soma (~125 μm)
source: While wild-type complex cells typically have peak sholl intersections of 8–11 around 200 μm from the soma, Lis1-MUT complex cells have fewer peak intersections (~7), closer to the soma (~125 μm) (Wt n = 10 complex and 14 simple; Lis1-MUT n = 10 complex and 12 simple).
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis using Sholl analysis

claim: There has been an effect of the Lis1 mutation, either direct or indirect, in stunting general morphological development
source: While relatively speaking, the complex and simple subtypes persist in the Lis1-MUT mice, there has been an effect of the mutation, either direct or indirect, in stunting general morphological development.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of morphological features between wild-type and mutant mice

claim: Resting membrane potential displayed a Pearson r value of 0.44 for correlation with position in wild-type litter mates, and an r-value of 0.07 in Lis1 mutant mice
source: Resting membrane potential displayed a pearson r value of 0.44 for correlation with position in wild-type litter mates, and a r-value of 0.07 in Lis1 mutant mice (Wt: n = 23, Lis1-MUT: n = 23).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrophysiological data

claim: Sag index correlated with position at an r-value of 0.5 in wild-type mice and an r-value of 0.05 in Lis mutants
source: Sag index correlated with position at an r-value of 0.5 in wild-type mice and an r-value of 0.05 in Lis mutants (Wt: n = 24, Lis1-MUT: n = 26).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrophysiological data

claim: Input resistance and depth in wild-type mice had a correlation value of r = 0.2, while in Lis mice r = −0.1
source: Input resistance and depth in wild-type mice had a correlation value of r = 0.2, while in Lis mice r = −0.1 (Wt: n = 23, Lis1-MUT: n = 26).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrophysiological data

claim: Many of the positional differences in physiological properties observed in wild-type littermates persisted or at least trended toward significant when sorted by putative cell type
source: In sorting recorded data by putative cell type, we noted that many of the positional differences observed in Figure 4A persisted or at least trended toward significant in wild-type littermates (complex cells are filled circles, open are simple; Resting membrane potential: Wt mean complex −63.3 ± 1.2 mV, simple −60.3 ± 1.2 mV, p=0.09 n=11 and 12; Sag index: mean complex 0.75 ± 0.02, simple 0.79 ± 0.02, p=0.25 n=12 and 12; Input resistance: complex 120.4 ± 6.8 MΩ, simple 149.3 ± 14.11 MΩ, p=0.08 n=11 and 12).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrophysiological data grouped by cell type

claim: Differences between principal cell sub-types for most physiological properties seemed substantially diminished in Lis1 mutants compared to normal mice
source: Some of these differences in sub-types were still detectable in Lis1 mutants, but differences between principal cell sub-types for most properties seemed substantially diminished from those in normal mice (RMP: mean complex −61.2 ± 2.1 mV, simple −61.1 ± 1.5 mV, p=0.96 n=10 and 13; Sag index: mean complex 0.78 ± 0.02, simple 0.81 ± 0.01, p=0.09 n=13 and 13; R input: mean complex 171.9 ± 13.2 MΩ, simple 123.3 ± 13.02 MΩ, p=0.29 n=13 and 13).
evidence: Statistical comparison of electrophysiological properties between cell types in mutant mice

claim: Out of eight morphologically complex cells in wild-type mice, six were found in physiological cluster 0 and the remaining two in physiological cluster 1
source: Out of eight morphologically complex cells, six were found in physiological cluster 0 and the remaining two in physiological cluster 1.
evidence: Results from K-means clustering analysis of physiological data

claim: Of eleven morphologically simple cells in wild-type mice, eight were located in physiological cluster 1 and the remaining three in cluster 0
source: Of eleven morphologically simple cells, eight were located in physiological cluster 1 and the remaining three in cluster 0, suggesting that these physiological clusters roughly correspond to the two morphological subtypes identified in Figure 3 for wild-type littermates (Figure 4C).
evidence: Results from K-means clustering analysis of physiological data

claim: The same clustering analysis in Lis1 mutants yielded uneven cluster counts, and no clear relationship between physiological cluster and morphological cluster
source: The same analysis in Lis1 mutants yielded uneven cluster counts, and no clear relationship between physiological cluster and morphological cluster (Figure 4D.
evidence: Results from K-means clustering analysis of physiological data in mutant mice

claim: Physiological aspects of cellular identity may become smeared or lost under cellular heterotopia before or to a greater extent than morphological aspects
source: The data indicate a loose relationship between morphological subtype and physiological subtype in wild-type animals that has been significantly perturbed under the Lis1 mutation - suggesting that physiological aspects of cellular identity may become smeared or lost under cellular heterotopia before or to a greater extent than morphological aspects.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of morphological and physiological clustering results

claim: Cellular morphology is less predictive of intrinsic physiological properties under the Lis1 mutation
source: Put another way, cellular morphology is less predictive of intrinsic physiological properties under the Lis1 mutation.
evidence: Summary inference based on clustering analysis

claim: PV-expressing basket cells preferentially innervate deeply situated calbindin-negative principal cells
source: PV-expressing basket cells preferentially innervate deeply situated calbindin-negative principal cells, while CCK-expressing interneurons have a similar bias, but for superficial calbindin positive principal cells (Lee et al., 2014; Valero et al., 2015; Valero and de la Prida, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: CCK-expressing interneurons have a bias for superficial calbindin positive principal cells
source: PV-expressing basket cells preferentially innervate deeply situated calbindin-negative principal cells, while CCK-expressing interneurons have a similar bias, but for superficial calbindin positive principal cells (Lee et al., 2014; Valero et al., 2015; Valero and de la Prida, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Both PV- and CCK-containing cell types have undergone superficial radial shifts in Lis1-MUT mice
source: Our data indicate that both PV- and CCK-containing cell types have undergone superficial radial shifts, that is, the cell bodies have moved toward the s. radiatum.
evidence: Observation from immunohistochemistry experiments

claim: PV-containing somatic shifts appear less severe than CCK-containing shifts in Lis1-MUT mice
source: Overall, PV-containing somatic shifts appear less severe than CCK-containing shifts, but in both cases a few drastically shifted somas were observed (right tail of dashed histograms).
evidence: Observation from immunohistochemistry experiments

claim: PV puncta had a modest preference for non-calbindin expressing principal cells in both non-mutant and mutant slices
source: PV puncta had a modest preference for non-calbindin expressing principal cells in both non-mutant and mutant slices. PV-calbindin preference: 0.74 ± 0.05 and 0.63 ± 0.11 innervation biases for wild-type and mutants, respectively, p=0.55, each point represents 12 cells from a slice, n = 3 pairs of littermates from three litters.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of inhibitory puncta from immunohistochemistry

claim: Non-mutant CCK baskets displayed a preference for calbindin-expressing principal cells that was lost in Lis1-MUT mice
source: Non-mutant CCK baskets displayed a preference for calbindin-expressing principal cells that was lost in Lis1-MUT mice. CB1-R-calbindin preference: 1.32 ± 0.04, 1.02 ± 0.09 for wild-type and mutant respectively, p=0.02.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of inhibitory puncta from immunohistochemistry

claim: In control mice, omega-conotoxin reduced monosynaptically evoked IPSCs to 52.5 ± 3.9% of baseline amplitudes in complex cells, while events in simple cells were reduced to 75.6 ± 8.3% of baseline amplitudes
source: In littermate controls, conotoxin reduced monosynaptically evoked IPSCs to 52.5 ± 3.9% of baseline amplitudes in complex cells, while events in simple cells were reduced to 75.6 ± 8.3% of baseline amplitudes, consistent with our observation that complex cells are preferentially targeted by CCK-containing interneurons (Figure 6D (left), p=0.03, n = 8 Wt and 8 Lis1-MUT cells).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from pharmacological experiments

claim: In Lis1 mutant mice, omega-conotoxin reduced eIPSCs to 48.2 ± 16.4% of baseline in complex cells and 60.2 ± 7.8% in simple cells
source: In Lis1 mutant mice this differential CCK-containing inhibitory input was not detected, as conotoxin reduced eIPSCs to 48.2 ± 16.4% of baseline and 60.2 ± 7.8%, for complex and simple cell subtypes respectively (Figure 6D (right), p=0.53 n=5 and 13).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from pharmacological experiments

claim: In control mice, omega-agatoxin reduced monosynaptically evoked eIPSCs to 42.01 ± 6.2% of baseline in complex cells, while events in simple cells were reduced to 9.5 ± 0.7% of baseline amplitudes
source: In control mice, agatoxin reduced monosynaptically evoked eIPSCs to 42.01 ± 6.2% of baseline in complex cells, events in simple cells were reduced to 9.5 ± 0.7% of baseline amplitudes, signifying that events in simple cells were more dependent on PV-expressing basket cell input (Figure 6F (left), p=0.003, n = 6 complex and 4 simple cells).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from pharmacological experiments

claim: In Lis1 mutant mice, omega-agatoxin reduced eIPSCs to 49.6 ± 5.8% of baseline in complex cells and 14.2 ± 3% in simple cells
source: In Lis1 mutant mice agatoxin reduced eIPSCs to 49.6 ± 5.8% of baseline and 14.2 ± 3%, for complex and simple cell subtypes, respectively (Figure 6F (right), n = 6 and 7, p=0.0002).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from pharmacological experiments

claim: CCK innervations are more perturbed than PV innervations in Lis1 mutants
source: In comparing both interneuron networks between genotypes, data suggest that CCK innervations are more perturbed that PV in Lis1 mutants.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of pharmacological experiments targeting different interneuron types

claim: Superficial cells have been previously shown to exhibit a comparatively higher level of excitatory drive during feedforward circuit activation (large EPSCs per unit of IPSC)
source: Superficial cells have been previously shown to exhibit a comparatively higher level of excitatory drive during feedforward circuit activation (large EPSCs per unit of IPSC, Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: Inhibition:excitation (IE) ratios were positively correlated with somatic depth in the PCL for wild-type littermates, but not Lis1 mutants
source: Inhibition:excitation (IE) ratios were positively correlated with somatic depth in the PCL for wild-type littermates, but not Lis1 mutants (Figure 6H; Wt r = 0.4, Lis1-MUT r = 0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrophysiological data

claim: Complex cells had lower IE ratios than simple cells in both wild-type and Lis1 mutant mice
source: When recorded cells were sorted by complex and simple morphologies complex cells had lower IE ratios in both wild-type and Lis 1 mutant mice (Figure 6I, Wt complex 3.15 ± 0.39, simple 5.7 ± 0.95, p=0.02 n=23 complex and 23 simple; Lis1-MUT complex 3.02 ± 0.49, simple 5.03 ± 0.76, p=0.03 n=21 complex and 17 simple cells).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data grouped by cell type

claim: Both wild-type and Lis1 mutant slices were capable of producing robust gamma oscillatory activity (ranging from 18 to 50 Hz), in response to application of 20 µM carbachol
source: Both wild-type and Lis1 mutant slices were capable of producing robust gamma oscillatory activity (ranging from 18 to 50 Hz), in response to application of 20 µM carbachol (Figure 7; Buhl et al., 1998; Fellous and Sejnowski, 2000; Fisahn et al., 1998).
evidence: Experimental observation from extracellular recordings

claim: Slices from Lis1 mutants produced slightly higher frequency gamma oscillations than non-mutants (Wt 24.9 ± 1.7 Hz, Lis1-MUT 31 ± 1.1 Hz, p=0.005)
source: Slices from Lis1 mutants produced slightly higher frequency gamma oscillations than non-mutants (Wt 24.9 ± 1.7 Hz, Lis1-MUT 31 ± 1.1 Hz, p=0.005 n=20 and 14, respectively) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of oscillation frequency from extracellular recordings

claim: Addition of WIN-55,212–2 (2 µM) did not alter the peak frequency of the oscillations in normal type nor mutant recordings
source: Subsequent addition of the synthetic CB1R agonist, WIN-55,212–2 (WIN) (2 µM), did not alter the peak frequency of the oscillations in normal type nor mutant recordings (Figure 7D)
evidence: Experimental observation from pharmacological manipulation during extracellular recordings

claim: WIN-55,212–2 caused a significant decrease in peak power in normal type recordings but not in Lis1-MUT mice
source: but caused a significant decrease in peak power in normal type recordings (Figure 7E), but not in Lis1-MUT mice suggesting that CCK-networks in mutants are less involved in gamma oscillation generation than in wild-type littermates (Wt +WIN 0.93 ± 0.03 vs CCh alone p=0.03, Lis1-MUT +WIN 1.02 ± 0.04 vs CCh alone p=0.69; n = 20 and 14 non-mutant and mutant, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of oscillation power from pharmacological experiments

claim: CCK-networks in Lis1 mutants are less involved in gamma oscillation generation than in wild-type littermates
source: but caused a significant decrease in peak power in normal type recordings (Figure 7E), but not in Lis1-MUT mice suggesting that CCK-networks in mutants are less involved in gamma oscillation generation than in wild-type littermates (Wt +WIN 0.93 ± 0.03 vs CCh alone p=0.03, Lis1-MUT +WIN 1.02 ± 0.04 vs CCh alone p=0.69; n = 20 and 14 non-mutant and mutant, respectively).
evidence: Inference based on differential response to CB1R agonist between genotypes

claim: Wild-type and Lis1 mutant slices were capable of producing correlated oscillatory activity between deep and superficial electrodes
source: Wild-type and Lis1 mutant slices were capable of producing correlated oscillatory activity (Figure 8D; Wt 394.6 ± 80.0, Lis1-MUT 394.2 ± 60.8, p=0.99 n=20 and 14).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of cross-correlation from dual electrode recordings

claim: Lis1-MUT mice displayed significantly less temporally correlated oscillations between the two electrodes (Wt: +1.01 ± 0.8 ms, Lis1-MUT: −1.8 ± 0.79, p=0.02)
source: However, examining the time-shifts obtained from cross correlation analysis (how far one signal is peak shifted from another in time) we noted that Lis1-MUT mice displayed significantly less temporally correlated oscillations between the two electrodes (Figure 8E; Wt: +1.01 ± 0.8 ms, Lis1-MUT: −1.8 ± 0.79, p=0.02 n=20 and 14)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of time-shift from cross-correlation analysis

claim: The separation of heterotopic bands in anatomical space or deficits in basket cell network connectivity erodes the correlated activity between the bands
source: suggesting that while both heterotopic bands participate in the ongoing oscillation, their separation in anatomical space or deficits in basket cell network connectivity erodes the correlated activity between the bands.
evidence: Inference based on cross-correlation analysis of oscillations

claim: Application of WIN-55 produced modest decreases in wild-type cross-correlation values but not in the Lis1 mutants
source: Application of the CB1R agonist WIN-55 produced modest decreases in wild-type cross-correlation values but not in the Lis1 mutants (Wt: + WIN 333.9 ± 71.9, vs baseline p=0.04 n=20; Lis1-MUT: + WIN 427.2 ± 84.13, vs baseline p=0.43 n=14)
evidence: Quantitative analysis of cross-correlation during pharmacological manipulation

claim: The diminished response to WIN-55 in Lis1 mutants suggests a diminished role for CCK-containing interneuron networks in the mutant mouse
source: suggesting a diminished role for CCK-containing interneuron networks in the mutant mouse.
evidence: Inference based on pharmacological manipulation results

claim: WIN-55 application did not have a significant impact on the time-shift between deep and superficial channels in either genetic background
source: WIN-55 application did not have a significant impact on the time-shift between deep and superficial channels in either genetic background (Wt: + WIN 0.68 ± 0.52 ms, vs baseline p=0.62, Lis1-MUT: + WIN −0.41 ± 1.23 ms, vs baseline p=0.21).
evidence: Statistical analysis of time-shift data during pharmacological manipulation

claim: Layers are in large part an epiphenomenon of neurogenesis
source: Collectively, these findings bolster the notion that layers are in large part an epiphenomenon of neurogenesis, as has been hypothesized previously.
evidence: Inference based on the collective findings of the study

claim: Layer terminology has a correlated genetic component in wild-type mice as it is likely to capture a related embryonic pool of neurons
source: Importantly, layer terminology has a correlated genetic component in wild-type mice as it is likely to capture a related embryonic pool of neurons.
evidence: Inference based on developmental biology principles

claim: When traditional studies refer to cellular layer, they are using it as a proxy for cellular genetic subtype, which is no longer the case in heterotopias
source: Therefore, when traditional studies refer to cellular layer, they are using it as a proxy for cellular genetic subtype, which is no longer the case in heterotopias (Guy and Staiger, 2017; Caviness and Rakic, 1978; Guy et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The present study identifies a crucial network motif, CCK-interneuron targeting of calbindin positive principal cells, that is specifically disrupted in ectopic calbindin PCs in the Lis1-MUT mouse
source: Importantly, the present study does identify a crucial network motif, CCK-interneuron targeting of calbindin positive principal cells, that is specifically disrupted in ectopic calbindin PCs in the Lis1-MUT mouse.
evidence: Summary of the main finding from multiple experimental approaches

claim: CCK and PV expressing interneurons arise from different progenitor pools, in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE) and medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), respectively
source: CCK and PV expressing interneurons arise from different progenitor pools, in the caudal ganglionic eminence (CGE) and medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), respectively (Butt et al., 2005; Fishell, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: CGE interneurons are developmentally lagged relative to MGE pools, as MGE cells are born first
source: Additionally, CGE interneurons are developmentally lagged relative to MGE pools, as MGE cells are born first (Tricoire et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: Later born basket cell populations (CCK basket cells) appear to be biased towards innervation of late born principal cell populations (superficial, calbindin expressing) in non-mutant animals
source: Notably, later born basket cell populations (CCK basket cells), appear to be biased towards innervation of late born principal cell populations (superficial, calbindin expressing) in non-mutant animals.
evidence: Inference based on developmental timing and connectivity patterns

claim: Basket CGE derived populations wait until the first post-natal week to form synapses on principal cell somas in the PCL
source: In fact, prior work has demonstrated that basket CGE derived populations wait until the first post-natal week to form synapses on principal cell somas in the PCL (Morozov and Freund, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: Non-conditional Pafah1b1 +/- mice were generated by breeding a Pafah1b1 +/ Fl line to Sox2-cre animals
source: Non-conditional Pafah1b1 +/- mice were generated by breeding a Pafah1b1 +/ Fl line to Sox2-cre animals, heterozygous mice are referred to henceforth as Lis1-MUT.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Lis1-MUT mice were often noticeably smaller than litter mates
source: Lis1-MUT mice were often noticeably smaller than litter mates.

claim: In the Reeler mouse, excitatory and inhibitory cells are produced in approximately the correct proportions
source: Groups working in a related model of cellular heterotopia, the Reeler mouse which has severely disorganized cortical and hippocampal principal cell layering, previously reported that excitatory and inhibitory cells are produced in approximately the correct proportions, that ectopic cells retain expression of their correct markers, morphology of cell types is generally conserved, and their intrinsic physiological properties are largely unperturbed on a network level (Wagener et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2011; Caviness and Sidman, 1973; Guy and Staiger, 2017; Guy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on the Reeler mouse model

claim: In the Reeler mouse, morphological development and orientation of principal cell dendrites appear stunted and meandering

claim: In the Reeler mouse, synaptic network development was remarkably intact, as thalamocortical and intracortical connectivity, cellular tuning properties to stimuli, and even animal behavior seem only minorly altered if at all
source: In the Reeler mouse synaptic network development was also remarkably intact, as thalamocortical and intracortical connectivity, cellular tuning properties to stimuli, and even animal behavior seem only minorly altered if at all (Salinger et al., 2003; Wagener et al., 2010; Wagener et al., 2016; Guy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on the Reeler mouse model

claim: Feed-forward properties onto PC subtypes in Lis1 mutants retain their relative excitabilities
source: From a broad perspective, this is in agreement with the present work in the Lis1 hippocampus, as feed-forward properties onto PC subtypes retain their relative excitabilities, and Lis1 slices retain their ability to generate gamma oscillations (Figure 7).
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the present study

claim: Lis1 slices retain their ability to generate gamma oscillations
source: From a broad perspective, this is in agreement with the present work in the Lis1 hippocampus, as feed-forward properties onto PC subtypes retain their relative excitabilities, and Lis1 slices retain their ability to generate gamma oscillations (Figure 7).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from extracellular recordings

claim: Higher peak oscillation frequency in Lis1 mutant experiments may reflect that CCK-expressing interneuron networks tend to generate lower frequency gamma, and when disrupted, networks become more dependent on alternative faster oscillation mechanisms such as greater reliance on parvalbumin cell networks
source: One possible interpretation of this result is that CCK-expressing interneuron networks tend to generate lower frequency gamma, and when disrupted in Lis1 mutants, networks become more dependent on alternative faster oscillation mechanisms such as greater reliance on parvalbumin cell networks.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of oscillation frequency data

claim: The higher oscillation frequency in Lis1 mutants may reflect biological differences in hyperexcitability that predispose these mice and human patients to seizures
source: These results may reflect biological differences in hyperexcitability that predispose these mice and human patients to seizures – further study is required to determine if more heavily banded hippocampal PCL regions in mutant animals have a greater propensity to act as seizure foci.
evidence: Speculative interpretation connecting findings to clinical phenotypes

claim: Timing differences in gamma-oscillations likely arise from the physical separation of current sinks and sources under Lis1-MUT heterotopia
source: It seems likely that timing differences in gamma-oscillations arise from the physical separation of current sinks and sources under Lis1-MUT heterotopia, and not as a result of the CCK-innervation deficit described above, as these measures were largely unchanged by WIN-55 application in normal-type mice, however, that possibility cannot be ruled out (Hájos et al., 2000; Soltesz and Deschênes, 1993).
evidence: Inference based on pharmacological manipulation results and cited literature

claim: The time-shifts under baseline conditions in the Lis1 mutants roughly mirror the physical inversion of PCL lamina under Lis1-MUT cellular heterotopia
source: It is worth noting that the time-shifts under baseline conditions in the mutants are opposite in direction than that of non-mutants. In that respect, they roughly mirror the physical inversion of PCL lamina under Lis1-MUT cellular heterotopia.
evidence: Inference connecting timing data to anatomical observations

claim: Lis1 mutant mice display severe cellular heterotopias in both cortex and hippocampus, developmental defects, hydrocephaly, and enlarged ventricles
source: Rodent brains lack gyri but mice heterozygous for the human mutant Pafah1b1 allele (Lis1-MUT, Lis mutants) display severe cellular heterotopias in both cortex and hippocampus, developmental defects, hydrocephaly, and enlarged ventricles.
evidence: Description of phenotypes in the mouse model

claim: Lis1 mutant mice have increased network excitability, lowered seizure threshold, and increased spontaneous mortality rate
source: These mice also have increased network excitability, lowered seizure threshold, and increased spontaneous mortality rate – features shared with the human condition (Fleck et al., 2000; Hunt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Heterotopias in area CA1 of Lis1 mutants have a tendency to fragment the single excitatory principal cell layer into multiple pyramidal cell bands, stacked vertically on one another
source: Interestingly, these heterotopias in area CA1 of the hippocampus have a tendency to fragment the single excitatory principal cell layer (PCL) into multiple pyramidal cell bands, stacked vertically on one another – transitioning the region into what looks like a primitive cortical structure with multiple excitatory layers.
evidence: Observational description of the phenotype

claim: Hippocampal researchers have proposed a system of parallel information processing being carried out among the intertwined circuitry of CA1, where-in preferential interneuron targeting acts to segregate information streams to different sets of principal neurons
source: Concurrently, hippocampal researchers have proposed a system of parallel information processing being carried out among the intertwined circuitry of CA1, where-in preferential interneuron targeting acts to segregate information streams to different sets of principal neurons (Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature

claim: The crude laminar structures resulting from faulty cellular migration in the Lis1 mutant mouse might reflect natural underlying patterns in local circuit connectivity upon which normal hippocampal function is critically dependent
source: It seems possible, if not likely, that these crude laminar structures resulting from faulty cellular migration in the Lis1 mutant mouse, might reflect natural underlying patterns in local circuit connectivity upon which normal hippocampal function is critically dependent.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about the relationship between heterotopia and normal circuit organization

claim: Mis-lamination is a shared feature of several human neurodevelopmental disorders
source: Clearly, mis-lamination is a shared feature of several human neurodevelopmental disorders that merits deeper investigation and may inform our understanding of normal hippocampal development and function.
evidence: General statement about neurodevelopmental disorders based on established knowledge

claim: Recent evidence suggests a preferential connectivity between principal cells and either parvalbumin (PV) or cholecystokinin (CCK) expressing interneurons, depending on the extrahippocampal projection target, somatic position of the principal cell, or marker expression of the principal cell
source: Recent evidence suggesting a preferential connectivity between principal cells and either parvalbumin (PV) or cholecystokinin (CCK) expressing interneurons, depending on the extrahippocampal projection target, somatic position of the principal cell, or marker expression of the principal cell, suggests an underlying blueprint in the establishment of hippocampal circuitry and connectivity that has been previously underappreciated in what otherwise appears as a monolithic excitatory lamina, the PCL (Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018; Lee et al., 2014; Nielsen et al., 2010; Slomianka et al., 2011; Valero et al., 2015; DeFelipe, 1997; Deguchi et al., 2011; Valero and de la Prida, 2018; Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: There is an underlying blueprint in the establishment of hippocampal circuitry and connectivity that has been previously underappreciated
source: Recent evidence suggesting a preferential connectivity between principal cells and either parvalbumin (PV) or cholecystokinin (CCK) expressing interneurons, depending on the extrahippocampal projection target, somatic position of the principal cell, or marker expression of the principal cell, suggests an underlying blueprint in the establishment of hippocampal circuitry and connectivity that has been previously underappreciated in what otherwise appears as a monolithic excitatory lamina, the PCL (Soltesz and Losonczy, 2018; Lee et al., 2014; Nielsen et al., 2010; Slomianka et al., 2011; Valero et al., 2015; DeFelipe, 1997; Deguchi et al., 2011; Valero and de la Prida, 2018; Varga et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference based on cited literature

claim: In subjects suffering from cellular heterotopias that survive into adulthood, cellular networks function surprisingly well and animals are often behaviorally indistinguishable from normal type littermates
source: Remarkably, in subjects suffering from cellular heterotopias that survive into adulthood cellular networks function surprisingly well and animals are often behaviorally indistinguishable from normal type littermates (Salinger et al., 2003; Wagener et al., 2010; Wagener et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: In the Reeler mouse model, cells in cortex appear to be relatively healthy and are integrated into the local network
source: In the more thoroughly studied Reeler mouse model, that displays severe cortical and hippocampal mis-lamination, cells in cortex appear to be relatively healthy and are integrated into the local network (Wagener et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2011; Caviness and Sidman, 1973; Guy and Staiger, 2017; Polleux et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The formation of functional synaptic connectivity has some innate resilience to mis-lamination
source: Collectively, the evidence suggests that the formation of functional synaptic connectivity has some innate resilience to mis-lamination and layers may play little to no role in the guidance and establishment of synaptic connectivity (Wagener et al., 2016; Guy and Staiger, 2017; Caviness and Rakic, 1978; Guy et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on cited literature

claim: Layers may play little to no role in the guidance and establishment of synaptic connectivity
